extracted.intended_audience: parents, librarians, teachers, and general readers looking for guidance on ALA youth media awards
extracted.subtask_description: A concise explanatory cheat sheet describing each major American Library Association award given for children’s and young adult books, including who the award is for and key eligibility/selection notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Newbery Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Awarded every year since 1922 to the author of the most distinguished contribution to American literature for children. This is usually going to be a chapter book and slants heavily toward fiction titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually a chapter book (occasionally a picture book). Must be American (originally published in the US). There are winners and honor books; see full winners lists for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Caldecott Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Given to the artist of the most distinguished American picture book. If the text is not by the illustrator, the author does NOT win the Caldecott – it’s only for the illustrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically awarded to standard picture books, though occasionally longer illustrated works win. Must be American (originally published in the US). Winners and honor books are listed each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Michael L. Printz Award (Printz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think Newbery, but for young adult books since 2000. Like the Newbery, there are way more fiction books that win than non-fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given annually to an outstanding book for teens; winners and honor books are documented. Slants toward fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coretta Scott King Awards (set)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of awards given to African American authors and illustrators that demonstrate an appreciation of African American culture and universal human values. Includes Author Book Award, Illustrator Book Award, John Steptoe New Talent Award, and the Coretta Scott King – Virginia Hamilton Award for Lifetime Achievement (given alternately to creators or contributors to African American children’s literature programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are separate winners and Honors for author and illustrator categories. The Lifetime Achievement award is given in even years to an author or illustrator and in odd years to someone who has made substantial contributions via programs or activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Mildred L. Batchelder Award
rubrics_metrics.description: For the most outstanding children’s book originally published in another language in another country and then translated into English and published in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Created to recognize translated works; used to contrast with Newbery/Caldecott eligibility rules which require original US publication. Winners and honor books are tracked annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Pura Belpré Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Named for the first Latina librarian at the NYPL, given to a Latino/Latina writer and illustrator whose work celebrates the Latino cultural experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are Winners and Honors for authors and illustrators separately, and the awards separate children’s authors from young adult authors — resulting in three winners and three sets of honors each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Robert F. Sibert Informational Book Medal (Sibert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given to an author and illustrator for distinguished informational (non-fiction) books for children and young adults; winning titles can range from picture books to several-hundred-page juvenile non-fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established in 2001; awards both winners and honors. Good for identifying high-quality nonfiction for different age ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Theodor Seuss Geisel Award (Geisel)
rubrics_metrics.description: An award for books aimed at beginning readers; criteria mentions books that 'demonstrate creativity and imagination to engage children in reading.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focused on early/beginning-reader books; relatively new (since 2006). Winners and honors illustrate what engages emergent readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Schneider Family Book Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Given to an author or illustrator for a book that features the disability experience (whether it’s a main character or a secondary character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a winner and honor books chosen for each of three age groups: young adults, middle school readers, and young children. Useful for identifying authentic disability representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Stonewall Book Award (Mike Morgan & Larry Romans Award for children/YA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stonewall Awards include a children’s and young adult category (the Mike Morgan & Larry Romans Award) specifically for literature that relates to the gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stonewall Awards have existed since the 1970s, but the children’s and young adult category was only added in 2010. Winners and honors are listed by year.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Odyssey Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Given each year to the best audiobook for children or young adults; the award is actually given to the publisher. It must be in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many picture books win in audio form. Note: award goes to publisher, and English-language audio is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: The William C. Morris YA Debut Award (Morris)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awarded to a debut young adult author (they may have written other books, as long as this is their first teen book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee issues a shortlist (up to five titles) in December and names the winner during the ALA Youth Media announcements. Highlights notable first-teen-book debuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award for Excellence in Nonfiction for Young Adults
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizes outstanding nonfiction for young adults. The award also produces a shortlist of up to five titles released in December ahead of the winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-explanatory focus on YA nonfiction; follows a shortlist-then-winner process similar to Morris.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Alex Awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Given to ten books each year that are written for an adult audience but will be appealing to young adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights adult books with strong YA crossover appeal; ten winners annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Children’s Literature Legacy Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Honors an author or illustrator whose books (published in the US) have made a lasting contribution to children’s literature and whose books demonstrate a respect for the lives and experiences of all children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has changed frequency over time (every five years, then three, then two, now annually). Formerly called the Laura Ingalls Wilder medal; winners can be living or posthumous.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Margaret A. Edwards Award
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to the Children’s Literature Legacy Award but focused on young adult authors — honors significant and lasting contributions to YA literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named for Margaret A. Edwards (nicknamed Alex, also the namesake for the Alex Awards). Lists of winners are kept by year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other ALA affiliate awards (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are additional book awards given out by American Library Association affiliate groups that aren’t announced at the Youth Media Awards. Examples include the Tomas Rivera Mexican American Children’s Book Award and the Sydney Taylor Book Award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These affiliate awards often focus on specific cultural or thematic representation (e.g., Mexican American experience, Jewish experience) and are useful supplemental recommendation sources; winners/honors are maintained by the awarding organizations.
